utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I notice that Mr. Naletilic is not present at this moment. Yes? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I have also noticed this, and I am surprised because I have not been informed of it, although in accordance with your order, that Defence counsel must be informed in case of failure to show up. However, I will ask Madam Registrar what this is about during the break. So we need not waste Court time. We are still waiting for an independent expert report on my client, rather, his state of health, which has not been completed yet. Another thing I wish to request, Your Honour, is to be allowed to go to the registry and look at the list expert doctors so that a truly independent expert can be selected and the expert opinion made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Madam Registrar will explain to you during the break about all those matters. Since we have the witness here, we'll proceed at this moment. Yes, cross-examination, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I have some exhibits which I will use which will be distributed at this moment by the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bos:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will ask you some questions. It won't take long. But if you could just bear some moment with me. And for my first part of the questions, I'd like to go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified that you were evicted twice from your apartment, and the first -- on both occasions, I'd like to ask you some questions. So the first time was on the 9th of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that day, how many soldiers entered your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were men I didn't know. I didn't know a single one of them. There were two or three of them, and there were others outside in the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've said that you didn't recognise any one of them. But isn't it correct that one of these men was a man named Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this occasion, was -- were any of your family members mistreated? Were they kicked or were they beaten, or were you mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one was. I was there with my wife and daughter, and nobody touched us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were other Muslims from your neighbourhood also evicted on this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Yes, there were some. What date do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, on the day that you were evicted.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was so upset, I really wouldn't know. But there were others, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be dozens or hundreds or ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who could count them? I have no idea. I didn't even know what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you testified that you were expelled to this area, Donja Mahala. How did they take you there? Did they take you by a truck or did you have to walk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to walk. It wasn't far, and we walked in a group. Nobody touched us, but, well, we had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were left off in Donja Mahala, where did you stay in Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a house, a family house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you return after 22 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went home. I wasn't mobilised, so I was able to go back and nobody had touched anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've already answered my next question, but I'll ask you again. When you came back to your apartment, was your apartment still in the same condition as you left it on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it in exactly the same state it was when I locked it before leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had locked your apartment when you were expelled on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they told me to lock my flat and to keep the key, and that's what happened. And nobody had entered it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's talk now about the second time you were expelled, which is on the 2nd of July. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of July, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers were involved on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were -- who could count them? I don't know the exact number. There were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of those soldiers at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again: Was a man named Ernest Takac involved on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have heard the answer, but since I've risen, the witness has already said he didn't know Ernest Takac, so the question was superfluous. However, we have heard the reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were strangers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this occasion, you were taken to the Heliodrom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your wife and your daughter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a man named Zijad Kavazovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to respond aloud, because he just moved his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know a man by the name of Zijad Kavazovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be that he was a person who lived in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, maybe we should go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I haven't risen too fast, but is that Exhibit 803.03?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a new exhibit, and I wish to comment on all this. I think I can comment before the witness, but if you say that I shouldn't, then the witness could go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could we hear the witness first, then we'll hear your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, but then my objection would be superfluous because I want to acquaint the Chamber with my doubts about this exhibit, and I wish to be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we hear it after we hear the witness. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, Your Honours, this document speaks -- the contents of the document mentioned my client extensively. He's not here today. They claim it's a new document. We've had, since our Defence case started, a multitude of new documents which we have never received in discovery. And perhaps the Trial Chamber can determine whether we're going to keep receiving these new documents, quote, unquote, which implicate our client. And I wonder, Your Honours, why is it we've not received these documents in discovery prior to this time. I think it's improper. And I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I haven't noticed that your client's name was mentioned in this document, and thank you for drawing my attention to it. But this issue is involving a general question of law, we'll deal with it after the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can finish the witness, if we're allowed to although I'm not sure if we can frankly because of what I'm about to say. I very specifically a few moments ago made it clear that I was concerned about the record of Mr. Naletilic not being present today. We were assured that we could proceed without him. Now, in the last five minutes, his counsel, both of his counsel, both Mr. Krsnik and now Mr. Meek has indicated that -- has raised a question, how can we talk about this document when our client is not even here? Now, we can either go forward without Mr. Naletilic here, or we can't. But we can't have it both ways. So if they are going to take that position, which they both now have, then I suggest, Your Honour, request that these proceedings be recessed until Mr. Naletilic returns, or until we have a written waiver from him, or until we have a clear indication from Defence counsel that they are not having it both ways. It's okay to proceed, but as soon as there are any questions asked that implicates them, it's not okay. That's our one response, Your Honour. When the witness is not here, and I do want to respond most vociferously to the statements made about documents in disclosure. But I don't think we can proceed, Your Honour, on the record, and I object to proceeding, let me make the Prosecution position very clear, I object to proceeding without Mr. Naletilic here based on the statements made by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I state for the record we can proceed without my client because I go by what I said in the beginning. It has nothing to do with my client but the manner of work of the Prosecution. Your Honours, this game which is played by the Prosecution goes on. We are served documents, shall I speak now, shall we wait for the witness to leave, which have no value at all. We do not know where they come from, what they are -- and such documents seems to fall from the heaven on the Prosecutor's desk day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'll give you time to raise your objections. Mr. Bos, I understand that you have another document which is also new, that is, P567.3. Does this document involve Mr. Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Are we back in open session? I think we can move back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the name of the unit of which Mr. Vinko Martinovic was a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you were imprisoned at the Heliodrom from the 2nd of July to the 20th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was your testimony yesterday that in that period you were never taken out for labour except on the 20th of August when you got wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of August, I was taken out. I said that yesterday, last night. I was wounded that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But listen carefully to what I say: Were you ever taken out on other occasions during that period for labour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your detention at the Heliodrom, were there any other Muslims from your direct neighbourhood who were also detained in that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, the school was full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But also with Muslims from your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's talk about the 20th of August, 1993. You've testified that on that day, you were taken out for labour. How many prisoners -- with how many prisoners were you taken out? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that I was there, and some others, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more specific if you say "quite a few"? Could you give an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Come on, I didn't count them. How can I know how many of them there were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you on that day were sent to the Carinski Most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was that day that I worked, that day I was wounded, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was at the Carinski Most where you got wounded. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right in front of Carinski bridge, a shell fell there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it also correct that you worked for the HVO 1st Light Assault Military Police Battalion on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For which unit did you have to work, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that it's not true that you worked for the 1st Light Assault if you say that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say anything. What did I say? I don't know those military -- nobody told me then where I was going to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the name of the soldier who picked you up on that day from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We dared not look up, let alone -- how can I know the name of the soldier or anything?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if you don't dare to look up, you could still hear maybe somebody's name. It's -- didn't you hear any names of persons who picked you up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I was not supposed to know anything. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why didn't you dare to look up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not supposed to look or anything. But I didn't really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P434, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: There's not much point showing him anything if he can't read it without his glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll have to read it to him, then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I know you don't have your reading glasses on you, so I will have to read out this document to you again. Witness, this is a list of orders, organised by date, that members of certain battalions picked up prisoners for labour. Now, if we look in the column which is on the English page number 0046 in the last digits, for the 20th of August, it gives five entries. Four entries are for the 1st Light Assault Brigade. And one entry is for the ATG Mrmak. Now, for the entries for the 1st Light Assault Brigade, in the last column, they have indicated the names of the persons who were put in charge, and these were the persons who would also pick you up, who would pick up the prisoners. They have indicated the following names: Ejo Mandic for the 1st Light Assault Brigade, Ivan Martinovic for the 1st Light Assault Brigade, Dinko Knezovic for the ATG Mrmak, again Ejo Mandic for the 1st Light Assault Brigade, and Meho Gosto for the 1st Light Assault Brigade. Do any of these names ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the name Ivan Martinovic, the father of Vinko Martinovic is also called Ivan Martinovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Martinovic, Mr., he was with me in the civil defence, what? You are asking me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, let me just ask you, Witness, did you see Mr. Ivan Martinovic on that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please, I really do not think this is all right. The Prosecutor tries to muddle up the witness as if Ivan Martinovic, the father of Vinko Martinovic, took prisoners for labour. Now really, this is not in order. I object to this of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think Ivan Martinovic's name appears on this list. I think the Prosecutor is entitled to ask some questions for the clarification of this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Exactly, and that was the main purpose I was doing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you see Mr. Ivan Martinovic on that day, on the 20th of August when you were taken out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. I didn't see any one of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot invent a description of what the Prosecutor is doing. He is asking if he saw Mr. Ivan Martinovic when he was taken that day, taken from where, taken to where, which Ivan Martinovic? I really think, I mean, he's consciously confusing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we understand there's many people with the same name. Maybe this is a different person. I think the witness has answered that question already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand, but no, no, he wasn't taking. I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you got wounded on that day, did other people get wounded as well, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I saw was that I had been wounded, and I panicked, and then I was taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 567.3, and I'll read it out again to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got my glasses. Who is going to read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know, Witness, and I will read out this document to you. Witness, this is a report from the warden of the central military remand prison, and it states the following: "Following the request of 20 August, 1993 by the 1st Light Assault Battalion of the military police, four detainees were handed over guarded by Meho Gosto. Upon their return, we have been informed that six detainees have been wounded such as" and six names are listed including your name under number 3. "And on the same day, -- two detainees were killed" and they list two names. Witness, it says here that the persons who were picked up, they were picked up by the name of Meho Gusto, and is it correct that's the same name that was mentioned before in the other document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- I don't know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions about after --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm too tired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm almost done here, Witness. Just a few more questions. Is it correct that after you got wounded and got back to Mostar, that you went to the Martinovic family to help you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that when you went to the Martinovic's, that you spoke both to the father, Ivan Martinovic, and to Vinko Martinovic himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that wasn't really clear from your testimony yesterday, but was one of the reasons that you approached the Martinovic family the fact that you and your wife were neighbourhood friends of the Martinovic family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war. We were neighbours, lived next to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: And still. We are still neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what kind of protection were you given? What did you ask for and what kind of protection did they give you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: First my wife was sick, and I can never forget it, in the war, that family helped me, Vinko Martinovic first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard already a number of details which could disclose the witness's identity, apart from the date which the Prosecutor read, he has also read several names including the name of this witness. Now we come to a string of details which can show exactly who that is, what went on to the -- what happened to the witness's wife. So if the Prosecutor intends to proceed, could we then go please into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we could go to the private session, but we don't see any trace of disclosure of the identity of this witness because we also keep a close watch on the screen. Yes, we'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if my learned friends makes an accusation that I mentioned the witness's name I would like to have that corrected because I didn't do that and I don't want to have that reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt you. You may continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned how Vinko had put something on your door. What was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name, and Stela put it on the door. It says that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he's left me in the flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he was guaranteeing your safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark. Questions by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have very few questions for you. I know you're nervous, and you said you were tired. Do you remember on the 9th of May, when the soldiers came to your house, do you remember if you don't just say you don't remember. Do you remember approximately when during the day that was? Was it the morning, the afternoon, the evening, or the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now that you remember that it was in the morning, was it early in the morning or had the morning well developed, like now, 9.30, 10.00, or was it earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never looked at my watch, but it was morning. Now when ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's fair enough. I know it's a long time ago. The other thing I wanted to ask you about is when you were taken to the Heliodrom, were you very upset and very nervous, which would be understandable, of course?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you think that's why you weren't asked to go out and work, or was there any other reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, they did not take people out. I went out only once. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, in the room that you were in, I think you said it was the classroom, were there any days in which some of your friends and colleagues were taken out, and you were left behind? Or are you saying that nobody was taken out until the day you were taken on the 20th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before. They took out people for work every day, and it was just kind of a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So your unlucky number didn't come up until the 20th of August. Is that what you're saying? A. Yes, yes. That was the only day that I worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions. And we appreciate your being here. It's not easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. We appreciate your evidence very much. The usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, now is the time for you to explain to us about your doubts on this document, P803.03.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. However, I feel as if I were playing Russian roulette. This is not something -- thank you. This is really like Russian roulette. Now things have turned out well, by "well," I mean the witness himself has stated that what is stated here is not true. However, had not the witness been here to deny this, the Prosecution would have waived this document about, claiming it to be true. There are three essential questions here: The first is that this document was produced by AID, at least that's what it says in the heading. This is a secret Muslim terrorist organisation now being investigated in Sarajevo. I have documents which are now being translated, and I will hand them over to the Court. This is an investigation against the director of AID, his deputy, and his second assistant. I have the whole file of the investigation, and the OTP also has it, but it keeping quiet about it. They have been accused of terrorism, of political assassinations, forging documents, and all this is being investigated by the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were arrested by SFOR. Their secret training camp was surrounded because it was under the auspices of the Iranian secret service and al Qaeda. These were typical products of theirs. The Prosecutor says that the source is the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, you still do not have my submission because I am now having translated voluminous documentation, which I will attach. You said that the two sides could express their stand points on the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I will provide my submission about this. I now simply wish to say that a government of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not exist. This place is no kindergarten. It's an international court. We cannot play cat and mouse here like little children. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not exist, and this is a well-known fact. Thirdly, Your Honour, this sort of statement, even were it true, the jurisdiction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of Croatia, of Serbia, of Yugoslavia, the Former Yugoslavia, would say that it cannot be used in court proceedings. It would be banned, forbidden by law. No police record or intelligence record may be used at a trial in court proceedings, either as evidence or least of all as grounds for a judgement. What is this about, Your Honours? The gentlemen from the OTP, seeing the strength of their evidence and their witnesses, are trying through the back door through a witness like this to say, yes, yes, we have a question here about Stela, and then they submit a statement which contains some mention of Stela, plus five pages about my client. And in this way, the Prosecution is piling up documents for you to read. And they are fulfilling their aim. Why didn't they bring Zijad Kavazovic as an OTP witness here, if he exists at all? I no longer believe anything, least of all the good faith of my learned friends from the OTP. I don't know if this Zijad Kavazovic exists even, it would be interesting to find out. And I hope, Your Honours, that God will help me and that somebody from AID will finally come here to testify, someone whose conscience will prompt them to tell Your Honours what was really happening behind the scenes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I promise to be shorter and less emotional than Mr. Krsnik. In terms of the document, sir, the document that Mr. Bos used was used for two purposes, both of which I believe are completely proper in our submission. It was used in an attempt -- it may have failed, but that's not the standard. But it was a reasonable and fair attempt to refresh the witness's recollection. It is indeed true that many of these events happened a long time ago. It is often the case, has often been the case in this trial, that when a witness is shown documents, they recall things they didn't initially recall. They may not recall something in the first document, it may take the second or a third document. But eventually they may remember. And the Prosecution is entitled to both probe, is intended to both probe and not necessarily take the first witness given -- the first answer given by the witness. The Prosecution is intended to ask questions several times, if it seems perhaps necessary, and with some of these witnesses, it is, either because of their memory or their demeanour or their concern about being in the courtroom. And the Prosecution is also entitled to try to refresh witness's recollections. It may ultimately fail or succeed. That is not the point. We are entitled to try. What Mr. Bos did was entirely in my respectfully submission entirely proper. It was also offered to the Chamber to show the basis for counsel's questions. There have been a number of occasions, even in the past few weeks, where both Defence teams have gotten on their feet very vociferously protesting about the basis of the questions of the Prosecution. Mr. Bos was very transparent in showing everyone in the courtroom the basis for the question that was put. And in my respectful submission, Mr. Bos behaved properly in every respect. We, of course, could not disagree more with counsel's allegations about AID and his statements about the Bosnia -- excuse me, the federation government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I told you now I will not belabour that except to say that we could not disagree more. And I think counsel should be very careful in the allegations he makes about terrorist organisations. In terms of documentation, sir, Mr. President, Your Honours, we do look for documents when witnesses come to testify. If a witness comes to testify, the Prosecution investigates our available documentation. And indeed, if we find the document that relates to a particular witness or part of their testimony, something that they have put in issue by their direct examination, then of course, of course, the Prosecution will seek to use it. And we will continue to seek to use it, and there may be new documents every day. There may be new documents every day. If counsel brings witnesses here, we have the right to cross-examine. We don't have any discovery from the Defence. We have no prior statements. We get nothing. We get nothing, Mr. President. When we hear the direct examination and we investigate what we may have, the information that may be available to the OTP about a witness, then we may use it, and if we deem it proper, we will use, subject to the Court's guidance. So to answer counsel's questions, yes, they are new documents. There may be new documents every day. There's probably going to be new documents later today, and there's probably going to be new documents tomorrow. And that is the way, respectfully, Mr. President, the process works. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we are not debating this issue, you know. We could spend a whole day here. I understand the views from the both parties. I give you one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May we go into private session, please. Because I wish to inform the Chamber about some other matters. I was not going to bring up now, but the Prosecutor has prompted me to do so. So I request that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, but you have to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, I think I have to hear your view on this document since this witness is your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour, for giving me leave to speak. The Defence has no documents to tender, but we have not yet heard from the Prosecution whether they wish to tender this document. If they do not intend to tender it, I have nothing to say. If they do, then I will have something to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We do not intend to tender this document, Your Honours. The only three exhibits which I intend to tender are the map, 11.18/17, the map as marked. And furthermore, Exhibit P56.3. And that will be an exhibit under seal, because it refers to the witness's name. Exhibit P434 is already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Seric. I think there should be no objections concerning that map, that is P11.18/17, which was marked and under seal. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour. And I will go further: I have no objection to the documents the Prosecution is tendering, and I have no further comment to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about that document, P567.3? No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It simply establishes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The accused Naletilic would object to the introduction of 567.3 on the basis that this witness knew nothing about this document, absolutely nothing about this document. 567.3 is being offered; 703.03 is not being offered. This witness was shown the document and knew nothing about the document. That's tantamount to not showing the document to the witness at all and then asking that the document be tendered into evidence. Mr. Seric doesn't object but we do object on that grounds. No foundation, no indicia of reliability. And even though the Prosecutor did not ask that 803.03 be admitted, give me 30 seconds, Your Honours, if, in fact, the Prosecutor wanted to refresh the recollection of this witness, this witness first told the Prosecutor "I cannot read, I don't have my reading glasses." He could have, as Judge Clark said, synopsised one paragraph on page 4, that's all he asked the witness about. That's all he wanted to ask the witness about. But the Prosecution it appears has a paragraph poisoning the well by putting a five, six-page English document full of insinuations about Mr. Naletilic in front of this Trial Chamber and then only asking about one paragraph which does not mention Mr. Naletilic. I think this practice is improper, and I think the Trial Chamber should ask the Prosecutor to cease this practice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the document P567.3, although the witness did not recognise that document, by his testimony corresponded to the contents of that document. Secondly, Mr. Seric has no objections to the admission of this document, and this is a witness for Mr. Seric. This document does not mention at all Mr. Naletilic's name. So this document is admitted. Well, I think we'll have our break. And during the break, I'll instruct Madam Registrar to make sure the waiver of Mr. Naletilic for our continued sitting on this case. We'll rise until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Our witness is here, but before he comes in, could I have a minute, please. It has to do with these maps. Perhaps you have noticed that several witnesses have complained, said that these Mostar plans were not accurate. And when they marked the localities they lived in, a number of witnesses said that names were not correct. We consulted our client, and he told us that the witnesses' objections were correct and requested that we stop using such an inaccurate plan. Why? Our witnesses says that the name of localities such as, Djikovina, Panjevina are marked erroneously so that the witnesses get confused. For instance, where it says Djikovina should be Ilici, because Djikovina is a bit lower. Where it says Panjevina that is where Djikovina should be. And what happens is that when a witness knows that a house, for instance, is in Djikovina, the witness sees how the map says Djikovina, and marks it there, although Djikovina is erroneously indicated in the map. So we do not know. This has not caused by particular problem for our Defence because one is more or less clear where the houses are located which they pointed at. However, these maps create a certain confusion and are inaccurate, and they could be challenged at some point. I looked at these maps which we were given by the OTP, and I have not seen a single map without such mistakes. Why do we address the Court? I want to ask whether the Prosecutor has an accurate map so that we could use that one. Now, we shall have a witness to whom I'd like to show the map, but in this situation, I just wonder, would it perhaps be better for me not to show him the map and have him describe certain locations are, or if I have to have this map, then I'll have to clarify these inaccuracies with him. Now, if OTP has another map, could we then have it, and could the Court please instruct me, should I examine the witness without a map or try to clear the inaccuracies up with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Par, to bring up this issue. Of course, we would like to use a map as accurate as possible, if they are available. And secondly, I believe that using this map is just an indication. We cannot only rely on the marks made by the witness on those maps. We also have to refer to the testimony of this witness according to the transcript at a later stage. So I believe that these maps can only give us a rough idea of the locations, not the exact places where he lives. So you may continue using these maps and see how far we go with these maps. If not, we just give this effort up. Yes, could we have the next witness. Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Before we begin, I'd like to tell you that the Court has granted you protective measures, that is, voice and face distortion, and alias, and we shall go into private session when we discuss some personal matters so that nothing will get out of this courtroom. But before we begin, you'll be shown a sheet of paper with your name on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the usher please give the witness this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If your name is accurately written, then you will just say "yes" without saying your name aloud, and then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During our conversation, we shall do our best to speak slowly. If you can, please, pay attention to this microphone. When you see that the red light is off, that will mean that I've switched off, and then you can start answering slowly so the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go into private session for a series of questions which have to do with the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we shall begin with the period of the Serb aggression against Mostar. But before that, tell me, did you spend -- were you in Mostar during the war? Have you been in Mostar all the time until this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Mostar all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb aggression, what happened to you then? Were you militarily involved, just briefly what did you do during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: No, I was not involved in the army because I was relieved of the military duty even in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did you do during that time, what kind of duties did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I repaired radio stations, Motorolas and whatever for all the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you do it? Did you go to these units, or did they come to your workshop or your home? Can you tell us just how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Well, at times, I would go out, but it was always in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it that you had to repair, what kind of equipment was it? Just as an example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Radio stations which would be captured during the Serb aggression, and I changed the frequencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your job wasn't of a military character; you were not militarily engaged. You were a civilian who provided this kind of service to different units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Vinko Martinovic, Stela, at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say how did you know him, on what terms were you with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Balinovac was a centre where the young people used to get together before the conflict, and that is how we came to know one another. We come from this very small area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of the Serb aggression, was Stela militarily engaged? Was he a member of any military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: He was in the HOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also do these repairs for his unit, for HOS? Did you go to him, or would he perhaps bring some of these appliances to you? Did you at that time have that kind of regular contact with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, I volunteered and placed myself at the disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the time of the Serb aggression, liberation from the Serbs, and shortly a conflict between Muslims and Croats broke out. Do you remember the day when the conflict started in Mostar? What day was it, and tell us, perhaps, how did you see the day? What happened to you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1993, the gunfire started around 4.00, or half past, early, at daybreak. I was at home with my family. And I spent there the whole day at a loss. I didn't know what was going on. I thought that the troops were firing between themselves, and I was not with the military. And the media was saying that the HVO should be placed under the command of the TO of the BH army, and in Bosnia, the HVO under the command of the army, of the Armija. And I thought that that was some kind of conflict between them. It would be over in no time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I understood you right, you spent the day with your family in your flat. Did anyone come to your door that day, any soldier? Did anyone come to try to evict you? Did anything like that happen that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: No, not that day. The next day, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But was anyone evict anyone else in your building, or is it that nothing happened to anyone that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: In my building and around me, nothing happened that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that something began to happen the next day, so tell us what was it, the next day, on the 10th of May, what came to pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: The next day, they came and requested to see our IDs and took the Muslims, Bosniaks, out, and then made us walk into a column and walk towards the stadium, towards the pitch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that? Do you know which troops were they? What was the unit? How did they take you out? What did they tell you? How did they take you to this pitch? Whom did they take there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: All the Bosniak families. I didn't know who were those troops. And I was walking by myself at the head of the column thinking if there's anything from Mostar, they will recognise me and turn me back, and that is what happened some 200 metres later by Milicevic, his troops. Two or three vehicles came up, they stopped us. And we talked with these troops and I said that I was their member and I was turned back. Which was not true because I wasn't. But that is what he said so that my wife and my children and I were sent back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you didn't know who those soldiers were, and at the same time you said that "I was at the head of the column thinking that somebody from Mostar would turn up." Does that mean that this unit that came to your place was not from Mostar? Do you know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Later on, I mean, when I returned, Baja came to see me and said that they were from Livno because in Mostar, about 70 per cent of the population know me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, Baja Milicevic turned up, and he knows you, took you out of the column, told them that you were his soldier, and you turned you back to your flat. Did others return home, or were you the only one who returned to his flat in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: The others were taken towards the pitch, towards the playground, play field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to those who were taken away. But that day, when you returned, when you returned, did anything else of significance happen to you, or was that all as far as your family was concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Within one hour or an hour and a half, I can be quite accurate, Vinko Martinovic Stela came because Baja had told him what had happened to me, and said that if travel troops came up to tell them that I was his soldier. So that meant I got tremendous support, and after that I was not too afraid any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Vinko Martinovic came to you on his own, after he had heard it from Baja, or did you call him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: No, Baja must have told him, or somebody else whom he had met because I did not leave the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us go back a little to the -- to your neighbours who were taken towards that play field. Did they ever return to your building, or was it that they left and never came back? Did those who were taken away on the 10th of May, were they -- did they come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: They spent at the Heliodrom, seven to ten days. That is what they told me. They all came back, and they were all together in the building. And then it was on a voluntary basis, that is, at the level of the town, it was -- the buses were organised. Who wants to go to the east side? Who wants to go abroad? Who wants to say? So some opted for moving over to the east side, others for being abroad, and some stayed. I stayed because I was not a soldier, and I enjoyed this protection, and I was not afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clear this up. So those same families that were taken to the stadium, returned a few days later back to their flats, to this building, had their flats been looted? Had they been burgled or did they find the flats in the same shape they left them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: At the time the flats were locked and nobody had taken anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a little bit about this organisation. You say that after that, people started leaving in an organised manner. Was it truly organised, meaning that one could leave of his own will, that people were given a choice, I want to go to the east side, want to go abroad, or do you want to stay? Or was it under duress?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: It was all on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some boarded buses or on foot, or did they all go at the same time? Or did first those who wanted to go abroad leave, and then those to the east side? How long did it last? Was it one day or longer? How was it all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: During -- in the course of a week, for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the majority leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Everybody from our building went, and from those small other buildings, small houses which looked like sheds, they stayed, and they are still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you did not leave? How did your family decide? Because you say that you were offered a choice. Why did you decide "we shall stay"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Well, I'm an electrician, a repairman. And all I'm interested in is that particular trade because I'm not a soldier, never served any army, I thought that nobody could hold me responsible for anything. And I simply thought that, no, that it was not necessary for me to go. And because Stela was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "Stela" rules here? Is it because his unit is there where you say "Stela ruled there"? What does it mean, does it have some authority or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: My house and his house are all within 300 metres diameter as the crow flies so that one of his folk would always be passing through. And this sector that he held, the front line that he held, everybody knew whose it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wished to say, then, that his unit was stationed in that area, and that that unit was connected to that part of town as other units were connected to other parts of town. Is this the explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, that's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So here is Stela, whom you know, his unit. You decide to stay because Stela is here. Why did you base your security on this? How did you believe that Stela could help you, or that he wouldn't harm you? Did you talk to him? Why do you say that you felt you could stay because you felt safe because of Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I knew Stela from before, and I trusted him. When he said something, when he said "stay, no one will touch you," you can come to me if you have any problems, then I knew there would be no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any problems in fact? Did anyone ever come to your door? Were there any attempts to evict you? Were there such situations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions. And Vinko Martinovic, Stela, saw this himself because he was in my flat with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say this happened on two occasions. Can you tell us about the first of these, tell us what happened. When was the first time someone came to your door to bother you or whatever they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: A few days later, four soldiers came to evict the Muslims who were left. Mladen Bojcic, a neighbour of mine sent his son to Stela's headquarters. The boy went there with his bike. Stela returned and surrounded the building with his men. He asked me where the soldiers were. He and his men came in and took these four soldiers prisoner and took them off to his headquarters. On the following day, when I went to the headquarters, I learned that they had been handed over to the military police and would probably be punished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more details about this event. Can you tell us the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: It was between the 15th and the 17th, about ten days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 15th or 17th of May, 1993. How many soldiers were there? Were they a unit or a group? What did they say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: The soldiers were all wearing military uniforms. I didn't dare go out, so I couldn't see who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, a neighbour of yours sent his son to fetch Stela. So it wasn't you, but another neighbour who sent his son. Do you know if that neighbour had any special relations with Stela? Was he a friend of Stela's? And what was he by ethnicity this neighbour who sent his son to fetch Stela?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted] he knew Stela from before because he had lived there for 50 years. He knew that Stela was a friend of mine and would protect me, which is why he sent his son to fetch him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time elapsed from the time these soldiers turned up to the time Stela and his men arrived and took them prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: About ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, were they all taken back to their homes? What did this mean for your whole building and you personally when you saw the fast intervention, the speedy reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Well, everybody thanked me, and they thanked Stela, although they didn't know him. But they told me to say thank you to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that these men were arrested, and that you heard they would be handed over to the military police and would be punished. Where did you get this information, when, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: On the following day, I went to the headquarters to do something, and I met three or four prisoners whom I knew well. On completing my job, I sat down with them and chatted because I was allowed to do that, as were the others. And they told me this, that the day before, four men had been handed over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about your going to the headquarters, can you tell us throughout this period, how did it come about that you used to go to Stela's headquarters, and did you go to the headquarters of other units? Did you continue to work on repairing equipment just as you did before the war? Why did you go to the headquarters, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I asked to go there, even if only to sit there, because I wanted them to know that I was attached to a unit, so I would not be evicted by others who came along because Vinko Martinovic, Stela, did not have a stamp, so he sent me to Baja, which is a hundred metres further on from Rondo. He sent me there, and they gave me a piece of paper saying that I was a member of that unit so that I could move around freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you talked to Stela and asked him to give you a document which would enable you to move around, and you were issued by a document not by Stela, but by Baja Milicevic. What sort of document was it? Did he really receive you into his unit? What did that document say and what could you use it for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: It was the sort of document carried by all soldiers. It said that I was one of his men, a soldier, and I could show it to the military police and other units to move around freely. And if there was a job for me to do, I was under an obligation to report and to perform the job. So I went to the unit every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a situation similar to that during the Serbian aggression, you were a civilian, you had this document so that you could move around. Were you issued with a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: On three occasions on the way from my house to the Rondo, on Bakamluk the military police arrested me and took me to the faculty, and I told them I was going to Rondo to the base. And every time, Baja came along to get me released, and after that they gave me a uniform, and then I had no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were given a uniform in order to avoid being arrested as a civilian and so on. Were you issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: No. Throughout the war, I did not have any weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a while ago that there was a second event when someone Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. came to your door. You have told us about one event; now will you tell us about the other one. When did it happen and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Some 20 or 25 days later - excuse me - from the beginning, every day, Vinko Martinovic would come and see me in the afternoon or in the late afternoon to see that I was all right because there were criminals around looting. So he would come to check on me, to see that I was all right. Some 20 or 25 days later, he dropped in with his wife. My wife made coffee, and we were just drinking coffee when four soldiers arrived at my door to evict me under orders from Vinko Martinovic, Stela. I told them that I was a soldier of Stela's and that I could not leave my flat without his permission, and they laughed at that. And then I went into my living room to talk to Stela, and two of them followed me in. And I said: "Men, let me introduce you to Vinko Martinovic, Stela, my commander." And they turn around and fled. I never saw any of them again. And I assume neither did he.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of them were there, and did you recognise any of them? Did you recognise the unit? Did you notice any identifying features?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I never saw them again, and as far as I can remember, they wore no insignia, only camouflage uniforms. There were four of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that they introduced themselves as coming on Stela's orders. When they entered your home, did they see Vinko Martinovic, Stela, himself there? Were they able to see him physically when they entered your flat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, they stood in front of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it then that they fled? Did they recognise him and flee, or did they not know him at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: They didn't know him at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they fled only when you told them who he was? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the only time you saw someone falsely introducing themselves as a member of Stela's unit and acting on Stela's orders? Did you have any other personal experiences where you heard or saw that there were such impersonations, not only in your flat but anywhere outside on the street, in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, there were many such cases that I heard about. And I personally witnessed one such event. May I describe it? I was in Stela's headquarters with the prisoners, and there was a meeting going on upstairs. He was having a meeting with his soldiers which went on for an hour or an hour and a half. And then a woman with two children arrived and she asked me is this the military police? And I said madam, what do you want? And she said: "Stela, Vrada and somebody else have evicted me." And I said when? And she said a quarter of an hour ago. I kept waiting there for 45 minutes until the meeting ended. And then I went to Stela and I asked him what was going on. And he told me. And he told me I should bring her to him. And he asked the women and she told him and told him everything that happen. And he gave her his hand and he said,"Let me introduce myself. I am Vinko Martinovic. Am I the one who evicted you?" And she said no. He said was it one of my men and she said no, and then he said do you have a place where you can spend the night? And she said that she had a sister who was married to a Croat. He ordered four of his soldiers to take that woman there, and put her up with her sister and then to go back to her flat and wait for the men who evicted her. He assumed the men would be back to loot the place. And they did come back. He took those four soldiers prisoner that night. I was in the headquarters until 3.00 or 4.00. On the following day I heard from the prisoners who saw all this, and they thought they were from the Sinj Battalion, and I heard later on that these men were sentenced to a month in prison each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: This was three or four months after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This woman spoke to you personally. Do you know what her name is? Do you know what she is by ethnicity? What part of town she was from? What did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: She is a Muslim. And she was from the area near the car association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She said that she had been evicted by Stela and some of his soldiers and she mentioned who the soldiers were. When Stela came out, did he try to establish with her whether any of the soldiers were actually his men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: She mentioned the soldiers by name. He brought all his men before her, because they had just been at a meeting so they were all there. He showed her the soldiers and told her their names, and she confirmed that it was not one of them. And then he asked if it was any of the others, the other soldiers. And the woman's answer was it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Not to repeat all this, he sent his men to her flat to wait in ambush for these four. They were arrested and handed over to the military police. Did that woman ever go back to her flat with her children? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He went to fetch her and he brought her back to her flat. She was taken back to her flat and she is still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he" went, did he do it himself? Did he do it personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I can't say that precisely, but it's thanks to him that it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any similar incidents? Did you see men coming to the headquarters to complain about something or to ask for help? I'm referring to Muslims, the Muslims who remained? Were there such cases? Was this something unusual or did it happen often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Whoever knew Stela would come to ask for food and other kinds of help. I personally distributed about 4 tons of food to Muslims. Vinko Martinovic, Stela, knew about this because he approved it. He told me to go and pick up the food saying it was for his men, and I distributed it to the Muslims who came to ask for food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling the Chamber that Stela authorised you to distribute food intended for the unit to Muslims who came to ask for food and -- how many tons did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: About 4 tons because the brother of Mladen Bojcic, a neighbour of mine, kept the records. And he said: "Well, you've taken a lot of food. You'll be held responsible for that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you say, you were there almost every day. Can you tell us how often you were at the unit? How much time did you spent there? What time did you usually arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I will arrive at around 8.00 a.m. And leave at around 2.00 p.m. Unless I went out on the field to fix a piece of equipment or a car. But I spent most of the time there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any prisoners of war there? Did you have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I did see them. I would sit there with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they came from? How they came to be in the unit, those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Those prisoners were brought from the Heliodrom at first, and later on, they asked Stela to spend the nights there because they were afraid they might be taken away by some other unit. So he said: "Well, there are some offices upstairs," and about ten of them agreed to sleep in those offices because they didn't want to return to the Heliodrom, so they slept there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the prisoners do there? What kind of jobs did they perform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: It was Sejo Peco who was a car electrician. And then there was one who have a mechanic, two other mechanics, Meho Ramic. They fixed cars if anyone needed a car repaired. They washed cars. They didn't do any hard labour, those ten. They ate in the same canteen as the soldiers and me. We often barbecued upstairs, and Vinko criticised me for that. He said we would set fire to the place because I took part in the barbecues. Since I was working, and Meho Ramic was a mechanic who repaired poker machines, I asked him to accompany me in the field and he asked to sleep in my home. And Stela approved this. So Meho Ramic stayed at my place and went around with me doing repairs and eating with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back a little. You are talking about the prisoners you used to see in the headquarters. They were there. They spent nights there. You think or you know that this was voluntary and that they asked Stela to be allowed to remain there at nights. Are you sure of this? And how do you know that they requested this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I know that because they themselves told me, and also because they asked me to intervene and to ask Stela to leave them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from them, were there any other prisoners? Were these the only prisoners who had good conditions? Were there other prisoners who were in a more difficult situation than this group that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I didn't see any other prisoners in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever go to the Health Centre where the demarcation line was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Rarely. Maybe just to fix a phone, but I never actually went to the line itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were prisoners of war at the confrontation line? Do you know if some of them went to the confrontation line or not? And if they did, what they did there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: In the first few days, perhaps they went there to pile up sandbags. After that, I didn't see that happening any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that some of the prisoners were either wounded or killed in the unit at the confrontation line or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me a little more about the conditions the prisoners were kept in. Were they able to receive visits if they had family in Mostar? Could they receive visits or go to their homes to see their families? Were there any limitations to this or special permission for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: These prisoners were not prohibited from doing anything. They can receive visits whenever they wanted to. As for visits, I myself took them home to have a bath but he didn't want to let them go on their own because he was afraid they might be taken prisoner by someone else or driven out by someone else and he would be blamed for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you asked Stela to let one prisoner go from the unit and spend the entire time with you. When was this prisoner released, this Meho Ramic that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: Meho Ramic spent six months with me. He never went to get any documents to be released. He was released when he came to stay with me. After the end of the war, he stayed on in Mostar for a year and worked there. When I left the unit and went to work at the mine, he worked with me for a year in Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a prisoner with you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologise for the interruption, Mr. President. Not an objection but I seek clarification, please. I was waiting to see if we might come back to it, but can we understand that the conditions of confinement that were being discussed in the last few minutes and the freedom of these prisoners are talking about the ten prisoners who stayed at the headquarters, specifically those ten prisoners we're talking about I suppose, I suppose, that might be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, you might ask some further questions to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have heard the question, but let's try again. Every day, you went to the unit. Every day you had contacts with the prisoners. Did you have contacts with only those several prisoners in the headquarters, or did you have opportunities to see all the prisoners who passed through, what they were doing, and how they were treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I went to the headquarters in Kalemova Street, but I also went to the headquarters in Rondo to fix things, and there I saw prisoners sweeping and cleaning the compound. At the confrontation line I saw them filling sandbags and taking them there. This group asked to spend nights in the unit. I think there were about seven of them. I can't be very precise. In the beginning, there were ten, but then he let them go home some of them. So the ones who remained were trained tradesmen who were able to fix things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We understand the conditions for those in the headquarters. Did you ever see any other prisoners mistreated, beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I didn't see other prisoners at the headquarters, so I can't say that that's so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the others you saw sweeping the compound, filling sandbags, did you ever see any of them mistreated or working in life-threatening conditions? Were shots being fired around their heads? Were you ever able to see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may mention a name, if we could go in private session, and then I will complete my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Witness, so this was your experience with Vinko Martinovic, Stela. Can you tell this Court briefly, how did you become a witness for the Defence? How did your testimony come about and why?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is my last question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MG
utterances.text: I saw in the TV news the indictment against Stela in The Hague Tribunal. And from my experience, I think that is not so, and I volunteered to come testify and tell the truth because within the context that he's described in, he is not that kind of man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
